description: The live NPC chat's CEFR adaptation over the World IR's `chatCefr` section (PL.native-chat-cefr-rows, slice 1): its vocabulary half, as replayable data. An engine runner answers every family from the section alone, with no model call and no key (corebridge/ENGINE_BINDINGS.md, `chatCefr`). (1) `worlds`: hand-written sections, each `{name, note, chatCefr}`; a section is `{version: 1, baseLanguage: 'English', levels, lexicon, messages}` (`levels`: a row per CEFR level A1-C2, `{npcLanguageModes: {bilingual, simplified, natural} percent, hints: {translationMode, showTranslateButton, translateButtonProminence, newWordHintFrequency, advancedVocabOnly}, vocabularyFrequency: {min, max (null: unrestricted), label}}`; `lexicon`: `{targetLanguage ({id, name, code, kind}, or null with a `reason`: no-target-language, target-is-base-language or no-language-record), reason, maxPhraseWords, entries, evidenceWords?}`, each entry `{word, key, translation, alternatives, partOfSpeech, difficulty, context, source, alsoEnglish?}`, one per key, in key order; `messages`: `{kinds: [{kind, role, startsWith, color: {css, rgba}, hints}], hints: {skipStartsWith}}`). The `earlier-shape` world omits `alsoEnglish`, `evidenceWords` and `messages`, as a section written before them does: an absent `alsoEnglish` is false and absent `evidenceWords` is none. The grammar check and the speech steps (`grammar`, `messages.speech`) are slice 2's and are not here. (2) `levelCases` `{level, row}`: every world's `levels[level]` is `row`. (3) `npcModeCases` `{level, npcId, hash, bucket, mode}`, read against the first world: `hash` is the 32-bit string hash of the id over its UTF-16 code units (h = h*31 + unit, wrapped to a signed 32-bit integer), absolute; `bucket` is hash mod 100; the mode is `bilingual` when bucket < the level's bilingual percent, `simplified` when bucket < bilingual + simplified, else `natural`. (4) `lookupCases` `{world, word, translation, hint}`: a word's KEY is its text NFC-normalised, U+2018 and U+2019 made `'`, every whitespace run made one space, the ends trimmed, every character at either end that is not a letter, combining mark, number or `_` (Unicode \p{L} \p{M} \p{N}) stripped, then lower-cased; an empty key finds nothing, else the first entry with that key answers. `translation` is `{word, translation, alternatives, partOfSpeech, difficulty, context, source: 'lexicon'}` from the entry, or null; `hint` (the hint card) is `{word, translation}` plus `context`, `partOfSpeech` and `difficulty` each only when the entry's is not null, or null. (5) `lineCases` `{world, why, level, line, state, mastered, hints, nextState}`: the hint rule over one NPC line. The line splits on whitespace runs into tokens; its PIECES are the tokens whose key is not empty. From the first piece, the longest run of up to `maxPhraseWords` pieces whose text (joined by single spaces) looks an entry up is one UNIT: a target word, or a HOMOGRAPH when the entry's `alsoEnglish` is true; a piece that starts no match is one unit: ENGLISH when its key is a word of the lexicon's English glosses (every entry's translation and alternatives split on whitespace and keyed) of at least `lineLanguageRule.englishEvidenceMinLength` code points, else FOREIGN when its key is one of `evidenceWords` or holds a character outside ASCII, else neutral. A new CLAUSE starts after a unit whose last token matches `lineLanguageRule.clauseEndPattern`, and wherever a token whose key is empty stands between two units. A homograph is a target-language word when the line GLOSSES it (right after its last token come one or more tokens whose key is empty, or a token opening with `(` or `[`, and then the next pieces, read past one optional `lineLanguageRule.glossArticles` word, key to its translation or one of its alternatives, a gloss of k words against the next k pieces), or else when the nearest evidence unit (target, foreign or English) in its own clause, or with none there the nearest in the line, is a target or foreign word; nearest is fewest units away, the one before first at equal distance; no evidence leaves it English. Each target-language unit (a target word, or a homograph judged target-language) whose key is not in `state.seen` is NEW: it is added to seen, takes `state.newWordIndex` (which then grows by one), and gets its hint card when the level's hint rule shows it: never when its key is one of `mastered` (each keyed); a word of null difficulty is beginner; when `advancedVocabOnly` only an advanced word; when `newWordHintFrequency` is 0 only an advanced word; else when the index mod the frequency is 0. A homograph judged English is passed over (no index, not seen). `hints` are in line order; `nextState.seen` is sorted by UTF-16 code unit. (6) `lineLanguageRule`: the line rule's three constants. (7) `messageKindCases` `{why, message, kind, color, hints}`, read against the first world: a message's kind row is the first of `messages.kinds` whose `role` equals the message's and whose `startsWith` is null or a prefix of its content as stored (absent or null content is ''); `kind` and `color` are that row's `kind` and `color.css`, or null for none; `hints` is true when that row's `hints` is true and the content starts with none of `messages.hints.skipStartsWith`. (8) `messageHintCases` `{why, world, level, message, state, mastered, hints, nextState}`: when the message gets hints, (5) over its content; otherwise no hints and the state unchanged. Every expectation was computed by the export's own rule (the writer of the section), never by this library; the rule is ported from insimul/babylon (Apache-2.0).
sources: pipelines c807d4e: pipelines/game-export/chat-cefr.ts (the export's rule over the section: translateWord, vocabHintFor, npcLanguageMode, vocabHintsForLine, chatMessageKind, chatMessageGetsHints, chatMessageHints and the line rule's constants), every expectation computed by it

worlds.name: constructed-tongue
worlds.note: A constructed language (no code): a two-word phrase (`tesh mira`), an apostrophe inside a word (`dor'ath`), an advanced word (`zhaltor`), an intermediate one (`varenn`), a word with an English alternative and a part of speech (`kesh`), a context note (`lune`), a capitalised source word (`Varo`), and sampleWords entries with no difficulty.

worlds.name: spanish-real
worlds.note: A real language with homographs: `once` (eleven), `sin` (without) and `red` (net) are English words too (`alsoEnglish`); accented keys (`dónde`, `mañana` with an alternative), a two-word phrase (`buenos días`), a two-letter gloss (`en`, in), a one-word key that also starts a phrase key (`buenos`, `buenos días`), a homograph with an English alternative (`fin`, end or finish), and the three difficulties.

worlds.name: french-real
worlds.note: A real language whose lexicon holds homographs (`chance`, `place`, `or`, `an`, `pain`) and target-language evidence words; `marché` is non-ASCII, a three-word phrase (`il y a`) sets maxPhraseWords 3.

worlds.name: cyrillic-real
worlds.note: A Cyrillic lexicon: keys keep every letter; a two-word phrase (`добрый день`).

worlds.name: vietnamese-real
worlds.note: Letters above U+024F and combining marks: a line written decomposed still finds the composed key (NFC).

worlds.name: no-language-system
worlds.note: A world with nothing to learn: an empty lexicon, reason no-target-language.

worlds.name: target-is-base-language
worlds.note: A world whose target is English, the base language: an empty lexicon.

worlds.name: no-language-record
worlds.note: A target language the world holds no record for: an empty lexicon.

worlds.name: earlier-shape
worlds.note: A section written before `alsoEnglish`, `evidenceWords` and `messages`: every entry is read as no homograph, there are no evidence words, and the message rows refuse it.

lineCases.why: A1 hints every new word; the phrase is one match (longest first); `and` is no lexicon word and takes no index.
lineCases.line: Tesh mira, ilo! Lune and kesh?

lineCases.why: A2 hints every third new word: indices 0 and 3 get cards, 1 and 2 do not.
A second meeting of a word in the same line takes no new index.
The state carries over: a seen word is not new; the next new word takes the carried index (A2: 3 gets a card).
A mastered word (keyed, so its case does not matter) takes an index but no card.
B1 shows only advanced words: zhaltor gets a card, the intermediate varenn and beginner lune do not, though all three take indices.
B2 (frequency 0, advanced only) and the same line: only the advanced word.
C1 (frequency 0, not advanced only): only advanced words still, since a frequency of 0 shows advanced words alone.
A word of unknown difficulty is beginner: at B1 it gets no card.
A curly apostrophe in the line matches the straight one in the key.
A comma inside the phrase breaks it: `Tesh, mira` keys to `tesh, mira`, which is no key, and neither word alone is one; only `ilo` is hinted.
An empty line: no hints, the state unchanged.
A line of punctuation only: no pieces.
The seen list is sorted by code unit, not by locale (uppercase-free keys; `dor'ath` sorts before `ilo`).
Accents and inverted marks: `¿Dónde` keys to `dónde`; the phrase `buenos días` is one match.
An English line using the homograph `once`: no target evidence anywhere, so `once` stays English.
lineCases.line: I was there once, my friend.

lineCases.why: The same homograph beside target evidence (`calle`, and the evidence word `la`) is Spanish.
A homograph glossed after a dash, read past one article (`— the net —`), is target-language even in an English line.
lineCases.line: Bring the red — the net — tomorrow

lineCases.why: A homograph glossed in parentheses (no separator token needed) is target-language.
lineCases.line: We fish with a red (net) here

lineCases.why: A gloss after a dash with no article: `sin — without —` glosses `sin`.
A homograph glossed in square brackets (a token opening with `[`, no separator token needed) is target-language: without the gloss, `net` (English, one unit on) would make `red` English.
lineCases.line: We fish with a red [net] here

lineCases.why: A gloss is compared with the alternatives too: `fin — finish —` glosses `fin` by its alternative, though its translation is `end`; unglossed, the English `finish` one unit on would make it English.
lineCases.line: We reach the fin — finish — today

lineCases.why: A clause end may carry closing quotes: `friend."` ends the clause, so `once` takes the evidence of its own (`amigo`), not the English `friend` just before.
Longest first: `Buenos días` is one match though `buenos` alone is a key too; the later `buenos` alone is its own match and new.
No separator and no bracket between `red` and `net`: no gloss; `net`, an English gloss word of the lexicon, is the nearest evidence, so `red` is English.
Clause rule: the homograph `once` after the `;` takes the evidence of its own clause (`amigo`), though the English `friend` is as near across the clause end.
Equal distance: the evidence before decides (`morning` English two units before, `pan` Spanish two after).
A non-ASCII word that is no key is foreign evidence: `está` makes `sin` Spanish.
Gloss words shorter than three letters are no English evidence: `red` with `on` and `it` only stays without evidence (English).
A gloss word shorter than three letters (`in`, the gloss of `en`) is no English evidence: the nearest evidence to `red` is `calle`, two units on, so `red` is Spanish.
A token that keys to nothing (`—`) ends a clause: `once` takes the evidence of its own clause (`calle`, two units on), not the English `friend` just before the dash.
A homograph judged English (its clause holds the English `friend`) takes no index and is not marked seen; `amigo` after the `;` takes index 0 and, at A2, its card.
lineCases.line: Once upon a time, my friend; amigo

lineCases.why: A1 with a mastered accented word given decomposed: keyed through NFC it matches `mañana`.
C2 (frequency 0): only the advanced `desafortunadamente`.
An English line with four homographs and English glosses: no target evidence, nothing hinted.
lineCases.line: Last chance, friend. Meet me at the place, gold or not, in an hour.

lineCases.why: A mixed line: the English `chance` is passed over; the French clause after the dash hints its words.
lineCases.line: Last chance, friend — dernière chance, mon ami !

lineCases.why: Evidence words: `bonne` speaks for `chance`.

English evidence counts the alternatives too: `tall` (an alternative of `grand`, no translation) before `pain` is as near as the evidence word `la` after, and the one before decides, so `pain` is English; `ville` is hinted.
A clause end may carry a closing guillemet: `friend!»` ends the clause, so `chance` takes the evidence of its own (`mon`), not the English `friend` just before.
lineCases.line: Good luck, friend!» chance mon ami

lineCases.why: A three-word phrase is one match (`il y a`), then `un an` makes `an` French by the evidence word `un`.

With no evidence in its own clause, a homograph takes the nearest in the whole line: the first sentence holds none for `pain` (`no` and `gain` are no evidence), and the nearest in the line is the evidence word `La`, so `pain` is hinted; `place` is French by its own clause.
lineCases.line: No pain, no gain. La place du marché est grande.

lineCases.why: A gloss with an article read past: `pain — the bread —` glosses `pain`.
lineCases.line: Le pain — the bread — est bon

lineCases.why: A2 hints every third new word: `mon` (index 0) gets its card, `ami` (1) and `grand` (2) do not; the bracketed gloss after a target word changes nothing.
Cyrillic words keep their letters; the phrase matches first.
A decomposed line finds the composed keys (NFC); the phrase `cà phê` is one match.
lineCases.line: Phở và cà phê ở chợ.

lineCases.why: A world with nothing to learn: no hints, the state unchanged.
An entry with no alsoEnglish is no homograph: `once` is hinted even in an English line (the earlier rule).

messageKindCases.why: A player line is user, whatever it says.
Role first: a player line that starts like a check-mark message is still user.
A system line starting with ( is system, and gets no hints either way.
The check-mark prefix (mark and space) is correct.
The Grammar Focus prefix is focus.

message.content:
📖 Grammar Focus: gender
Correct form: "la calle"

messageKindCases.why: The check mark without its space is an NPC line.
Half of the Focus prefix is an NPC line.
Content is read untrimmed: a leading space before the tip prefix makes an NPC line.
An NPC line is npc and gets hints.
An NPC line starting with ( is npc but gets no hints.

message.content: (Try one of the words I used.)

messageKindCases.why: A ( after a leading space keeps the hints.
An empty NPC line is npc with hints.
Null content is the empty string.
Absent content is the empty string.
A role outside user, assistant and system has no kind.
Roles are exact: `Assistant` has no kind.

messageHintCases.why: An NPC line gets the line rule over its content.
The same words from the player: no hints, the state unchanged.
A system line: no hints, state unchanged.
An NPC aside starting with (: it meets no word.
A tip naming lexicon words: none.
A leading space before (: the line is read.
A role with no kind: no hints, state unchanged.
A mixed NPC line in French at A2 with a carried state: the English homograph takes no index.

message.content: Last chance, friend — dernière chance, mon ami !

messageHintCases.why: Null content on an NPC line: no words, the state unchanged by the line rule.
